 CAT Chandigarh Sets Aside EPFO Officer’s Suspension And Chennai Transfer Over WhatsApp Group Messages
 By Priyanka Jha 
 23 October 2026, 2:52 PM 23 October 2026, 2:52 PM 
 4 min read 
 Share 
 X (Twitter) 
 WhatsApp 
 Facebook 
 LinkedIn 
 Email 
 Messages that the suspension order never mentioned could not be used to defend it, the Central Administrative Tribunal has ruled, setting aside the suspension of an EPFO officer and his shift to Chennai. 
 Chandigarh: Reasons that appear nowhere in an order cannot be added later to save it. On that footing, the Chandigarh Bench of the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) has quashed the suspension of a Regional Provident Fund Commissioner of the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), along with the fixing of his headquarters at Chennai about 2,500 km away. The justification built on his WhatsApp group messages did not appear in the suspension order itself [Kumar Punit v. Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation and Others] .
 Judicial Member Ramesh Singh Thakur pronounced the order on October 14, 2026, a week after reserving it on October 7, 2026.
 An order is judged by what it says 
 The suspension order made no mention of the WhatsApp exchange. The Tribunal therefore leaned on the Supreme Court’s ruling in Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner (1978) 1 SCC 405, under which the validity of an order must be judged by the reasons it records and cannot be supplemented by fresh reasons in an affidavit. It also drew on two High Court rulings on workplace WhatsApp groups, one by the Madras High Court recognising a “right to vent” and group privacy, and one by the Madhya Pradesh High Court.
 “In the circumstances pleaded before this Tribunal, and in the absence of any demonstrated rule or instruction governing such exchanges, the alleged messages, by themselves, cannot furnish a sufficient basis to sustain the impugned suspension. This is particularly so when the explanation furnished by the respondents does not find expression in the impugned order of suspension itself.”
 ALSO READ: CAT Allahabad: WhatsApp ‘OK’ Not Proof Of Sanctioned Leave, Tribunal Upholds Railway Employee’s Transfer To Fatehpur 
 2,500 km from Chandigarh 
 The Tribunal accepted that EPFO employees are liable to serve anywhere in India. That general liability, it said, does not justify a particular distant headquarters during suspension. Government instructions treat the last place of duty as the normal headquarters, and allow a change in public interest. Neither the suspension order nor the later order rejecting his representation identified any exigency or public interest, or explained how his staying at Chandigarh would prejudice the proceedings.
 The officer and the CBI case 
 The applicant, Kumar Punit, joined as Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner in 2014 and has been Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-I at Chandigarh since March 2024. He was named as accused No. 20 in a second supplementary chargesheet in a CBI case on alleged fraudulent settlement of provident fund and pension claims. A Special Judge discharged him and other EPFO officials on March 18, 2026, and the Delhi High Court dismissed the CBI’s revision petition on July 17, 2026. A separate charge memorandum on the same incident, issued on March 30, 2026, is pending and was not challenged in this application.
 On July 27, 2026, the Chairman of the Central Board of Trustees (EPF) placed him under suspension, stating only that disciplinary proceedings were contemplated, and fixed his headquarters at the Zonal Office in Chennai and Puducherry. The Tribunal stayed that order on August 7 and directed that he continue at Chandigarh.
 Vendetta alleged, remarks cited 
 The applicant alleged personal vendetta, pointing to a legal notice he sent on July 26 to an Additional Central Provident Fund Commissioner alleging defamatory conduct. He said no material showed misconduct and the order recorded no public interest for moving him 2,500 km away.
 EPFO denied this. It said that after the CBI arrested an Enforcement Officer at Patiala on July 22, the Central Provident Fund Commissioner (CPFC) posted an anti-corruption advisory in an official WhatsApp group, and that the applicant allegedly replied with remarks that were derogatory and questioned the CPFC’s authority, including “This is just tip of ice berg”. EPFO added that the legal notice reached the Head Office only on July 28, a day after the suspension. These are the parties’ contentions, and the Tribunal made no finding that the messages amounted to misconduct.
 ALSO READ: Chinnaswamy Stampede Fallout: ACP Vikash Kumar Reinstated, Karnataka Govt Tells High Court 
 What the Tribunal ordered 
 The application was allowed. The Tribunal quashed the July 27 suspension order and the August 15 order rejecting his representation, made the interim order absolute, and directed EPFO to let him continue at his last place of posting, Chandigarh, in accordance with law. There was no order as to costs.
 What the ruling adds 
 The decision applies a basic rule of administrative law to service matters: the State must defend a suspension on the grounds recorded in the order, not on explanations that arrive in the written statement. It also adds to the growing case law that treats informal chat-group remarks with caution where no rule governs such forums.
 Case Title: Kumar Punit v. Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation and Others [O.A. No. 060/984/2026] 
 Bench: Member (J) Ramesh Singh Thakur, Central Administrative Tribunal, Chandigarh Bench 
 Date of Order: October 14, 2026 
 Appearances: Senior Advocate Arvind Moudgil with Advocates Barjesh Mittal, Abhay Gupta, Harsh Pratap Singh and Yandasi for the applicant; Senior Advocate G.S. Bal with Advocate Aseem Rai for EPFO
